item.title: Dialectical variations
item.description:
Source: TW

There was dialectical variation among the early MIA Prakrits even at the time of Aśoka, so Aśoka used slightly different MIA variants in different regions. However, these inscriptions ultimately reflect actual spoken 3rd century BC MIA dialects.

It is “Pāli” and “Prakrit” which are literary composites.

There are 31 ways to say “he/she/it shall be” (bhaviṣyánti) in “Prakrit”: hohinti, hohinte, hohire, hossanti, hossante, hoihinti, hoihinte, hoihire, hoehinti, hoehinte, hoehire, hoissanti , hoissante, hoessanti, hoessante, hojjahinti, hojjahinte, hojjahire, hojjāhinti, hojjāhinte, hojjāhire, hojja, hojjā, hoejjahinti, hoejjahinte, hoejjahire, hoejjāhinti, hoejjāhinte, hoejjāhire, hoejja, hoejjā.

item.title: GAthA saptashatI
item.description:
Source: TW

Antiquity

But regardless on one’s position regarding authorship of the text, it’s undeniable that the anthology in question (Sattasaī) represents one of the earliest extant works in Mahārāṣṭrī and hence serves as a good point of reference.

Bāṇa refers to a kośa of songs of Sātavāhana, so some form of Sātavāhana “Gāhā” anthology likely existed at the time of Bāṇabhaṭṭa.

However, this anthology referenced by Bāṇa was not identical to the Gāhāsattasaī, which bears interpolations from as late as the eighth century AD.

item.title: Sanskritization
item.description:
Source: TW

Yet heavy Sanskritization of NIA languages in general is visible even in Diṅgaḷ poetry and the poems of Vidyāpati. Sanskrit loans in NIA were normalized very early.

Entire expressions were loaned. To use examples from Tulsīdās:

suni prabhu parama sarala kapi bānī।
“evam astu” taba kaheu bhavānī॥
kahañ kosalādhīsa “dvau” bhrātā।
dhanvī sakala-loka-bikhyātā॥

The phrase “evam astu” comes directly from Sanskrit. The word “dvau” (two) is not Prakrit. It is pure Sanskrit.
